item.title: EFL executive pay rises to $3.76M in 2025
item.description: Compensation paid to Energy Fiji Limited’s (EFL) key management personnel increased to $3.756 million in 2025, according to the company’s 2025 Annual Report recently tabled in Parliament. The report shows total remuneration for the Chief Executive Officer and Executive Management Group rose from $3.309 million in 2024 to $3.756 million in 2025, an increase of $447,000, or about 13.5 per cent.
item.content:encoded:
Compensation paid to Energy Fiji Limited’s (EFL) key management personnel increased to $3.756 million in 2025, according to the company’s 2025 Annual Report recently tabled in Parliament.

The report shows total remuneration for the Chief Executive Officer and Executive Management Group rose from $3.309 million in 2024 to $3.756 million in 2025, an increase of $447,000, or about 13.5 per cent.

Salary, performance pay and allowances accounted for $3.445 million, up from $3.033 million the previous year.

Superannuation contributions also increased, rising from $276,000 in 2024 to $311,000 in 2025.

The report identifies the Chief Executive Officer and Executive Management Group as the company’s key management personnel responsible for planning, directing and controlling EFL’s operations.

Fatiaki Gibson was appointed Chief Executive Officer in April 2025.

The executive management team also includes Deputy Chief Executive Officer Mitsuhiro Takeshita, Chief Operating Officer Bobby Naimawi, Chief Financial Officer Semisi Tawake, General Manager Generation Epeli Malo, General Manager Customer Services Annabel Ducia, General Manager Network Jitendra V. Kumar, General Manager Human Resources Randhir Charan, General Manager System Planning and Control Naomi Baleca, General Manager Information Technology Jiten Singh, and General Manager Special Projects Krishneel Prasad.

The annual report also details changes to the EFL Board during the year.

Rokoseru Nabalarua served as Chairman, while Mitsuhiro Takeshita joined the Board in June 2025 and Toshiyuki Suzuki was appointed in September 2025.

During the year, Fatiaki Gibson resigned as a director in March 2025, while Chitoshi Fukuda resigned in August 2025 and Tsutomu Fujita stepped down in June 2025.

Director fees paid during 2025 totalled $68,250, compared with $46,542 in 2024.

item.title: Registered voters reach 707,982 after latest roll update
item.description: The Fijian Elections Office (FEO) says the country’s National Register of Voters now stands at 707,982 registered voters, following its latest update completed in January 2026. Figures released by the FEO show the latest exercise reviewed data covering the period July to December 2025.
item.content:encoded:
The Fijian Elections Office (FEO) says the country’s National Register of Voters now stands at 707,982 registered voters, following its latest update completed in January 2026.

Figures released by the FEO show the latest exercise reviewed data covering the period July to December 2025.

During the update, 3,442 deceased persons were removed from the register, 484 individuals were flagged as inmates, 34 voters were reinstated and two people were removed after renouncing their Fijian citizenship.

The latest update follows a series of voter roll verification exercises conducted since July 2023.

According to the data, the number of registered voters has generally increased over the period, rising from 695,435 in July 2023 to 707,982 in January 2026, despite ongoing efforts to remove deceased voters and update the register.

Since July 2023, the FEO has removed a total of 30,123 deceased persons from the National Register of Voters.

Over the same period, 733 individuals have been flagged as inmates, 190 voters have been reinstated after verification, and 10 people have been removed after renouncing their Fijian citizenship.

The FEO noted that its July 2025 verification exercise included a four-phase deceased voter verification process using information from the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registry (BDM), the Fiji National Provident Fund (FNPF), the Provisional Voters List (PVL) together with Turaga ni Koro and next-of-kin verification.

The office said the BDM and FNPF data used in that exercise covered records from 2012 to June 2025 as part of efforts to maintain the accuracy and integrity of the National Register of Voters.

item.title: Bainivalu and Chaudhry trade barbs
item.description: A war of words has erupted between Forestry Minister Alitia Bainivalu and former Prime Minister Mahendra Chaudhry, with both exchanging sharp criticisms over government spending, accountability and support for cane farmers. In a social media post, Ms Bainivalu accused Mr Chaudhry of relying on personal attacks instead of offering solutions for Fiji’s future.
item.content:encoded:
A war of words has erupted between Forestry Minister Alitia Bainivalu and former Prime Minister Mahendra Chaudhry, with both exchanging sharp criticisms over government spending, accountability and support for cane farmers.

In a social media post, Ms Bainivalu accused Mr Chaudhry of relying on personal attacks instead of offering solutions for Fiji’s future.

“Mahendra Chaudhry’s latest personal attack is yet another example of the old politics he has practised for more than three decades,” she said.

“Instead of debating policies or offering solutions for Fiji’s future, he chooses personal attacks. That is the politics of yesterday.”

The Minister said Mr Chaudhry should reflect on his own record before criticising others.

“Mr Chaudhry should remember that the people of Fiji know his record. Before Mr Chaudhry lectures anyone about accountability or the proper use of taxpayers’ money, he should first answer for his own record.”

Ms Bainivalu said she remained focused on delivering for the country rather than engaging in political disputes.

“Mr Chaudhry is free to continue fighting yesterday’s political battles. I am focused on building tomorrow’s Fiji that is creating opportunities, strengthening our economy, and delivering for ordinary Fijians.”

She added that voters would ultimately judge the performance of political leaders.

“The people of Fiji know the difference between old politics and responsible leadership. They know the difference between personal attacks and real results. Ultimately, they will decide whose record deserves their trust and confidence.”

Responding in a separate statement, Mr Chaudhry rejected the Minister’s comments and accused the Coalition Government of excessive spending.

“Throwing stones while living in a glass house, Bainivalu?” he said.

Mr Chaudhry claimed the Government’s record on public expenditure was “quite shameful” and criticised Ms Bainivalu for supporting the parliamentary salary increase.

“She voted for the parliamentary salary increase at a time when her government had raised VAT to 15%, worsening the hardship already faced by ordinary people.”

He also pointed to ministerial benefits, including the purchase of duty-free vehicles, government transport and business-class travel.

Turning to the sugar industry, Mr Chaudhry criticised the Minister’s comments regarding cane growers.

“From that comfortable position she tells cane farmers they should have accepted $85 a tonne as guaranteed minimum cane price which was set eight years ago, since when costs have escalated by over 50%.”

He said ministers would eventually have to face the same farmers during election campaigning.

“These same ministers will later travel the country asking those same farmers for their votes. They are waiting to receive you, Minister!”

item.title: EFL signs deal for solar and battery project
item.description: Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Neoteric Investments (Fiji) Pte Limited to advance the development of a major grid-connected solar power plant and battery energy storage system in Ba. The agreement, signed on Friday establishes a framework for both parties to complete the technical, commercial, financial, environmental and regulatory assessments requir
item.content:encoded:
Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Neoteric Investments (Fiji) Pte Limited to advance the development of a major grid-connected solar power plant and battery energy storage system in Ba.

The agreement, signed on Friday establishes a framework for both parties to complete the technical, commercial, financial, environmental and regulatory assessments required before entering into a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA).

If completed, the project could deliver up to 100 megawatts of solar photovoltaic generation supported by a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), helping strengthen Fiji’s electricity network, improve energy security and support the country’s transition to renewable energy.

Under the agreement, EFL and Neoteric aim to finalise the Power Purchase Agreement within the next six months, subject to due diligence and regulatory approvals. Construction is expected to begin immediately after financial close, with commissioning targeted within 24 months, or earlier if possible.

EFL Chief Executive Officer Fatiaki Gibson said the agreement marked another significant step towards achieving Fiji’s renewable energy goals.

“This agreement reflects the confidence that private investors continue to place in Fiji and in EFL’s long-term renewable energy programme,” Mr Gibson said.

“More importantly, it demonstrates that our strategy is moving beyond planning into implementation through genuine partnerships that will deliver real infrastructure and long-term benefits for our customers.”

Mr Gibson said the proposed development forms part of EFL’s broader investment programme, which includes transmission upgrades, hydropower projects, solar generation, battery storage and modernisation of the national electricity grid.

“We are working closely with Government, development partners, financiers and the private sector to build an electricity system that is more reliable, more resilient and increasingly powered by renewable energy.”

“Every milestone achieved brings us closer to delivering affordable, secure and sustainable electricity for future generations,” he said.

EFL said the final size and configuration of the project will be confirmed following detailed technical and commercial assessments to ensure it delivers long-term value for electricity customers.

item.title: Teacher workload row
item.description: THE Fiji Teachers Union (FTU) has condemned an application from the Ministry of Civil Service to the education sector that allegedly could lead to teachers taking on more responsibility. FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said while cost-saving measures may be workable in some parts of the public service, they were simply not practical in our schools.
item.content:encoded:
THE Fiji Teachers Union (FTU) has condemned an application from the Ministry of Civil Service to the education sector that allegedly could lead to teachers taking on more responsibility.

FTU general secretary Muniappa Goundar said while cost-saving measures may be workable in some parts of the public service, they were simply not practical in our schools.

“Teaching is not an office-based function where duties can be redistributed through multitasking,” he said.

“A teacher cannot effectively teach two or more classes simultaneously without compromising the quality of education and student learning.

“The Circular 39 restrictions on acting appointments and the withholding of acting allowances are unacceptable.

“Where teachers are required to perform the duties and responsibilities of a higher position, they must receive formal acting appointment letters and the appropriate acting allowance.”

He said the Employment Relations Act 2007 promotes fair employment practices and employees should not be expected to undertake higher responsibilities without appropriate recognition and remuneration.

“Requiring teachers to shoulder additional responsibilities without compensation is unfair and undermines morale.

“The Government has also announced a freeze on appointments across the public service.

“Such a policy is particularly damaging for the Ministry of Education. Vacant leadership and teaching positions cannot simply remain unfilled while existing teachers absorb the workload.

“These positions are already provided for in the National Budget, and acting arrangements attract only a proportion of the salary difference.

“There is, therefore, no sound justification for denying legitimate acting appointments where operational needs clearly exist.”

Mr Goundar added teachers were already leaving Fiji in significant numbers in search of better opportunities.

item.title: Fiji eyes $500m package for economic reforms
item.description: FIJI is expected to receive a combined $US230million (about $F500million) in budget support financing from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) and the World Bank. The funding is aimed at helping Government strengthen its finances, improve climate and disaster resilience and advance key reforms before moving into major infrastructure investments.
item.content:encoded:
FIJI is expected to receive a combined $US230million (about $F500million) in budget support financing from the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) and the World Bank.

The funding is aimed at helping Government strengthen its finances, improve climate and disaster resilience and advance key reforms before moving into major infrastructure investments.

The package comprises $US80million from the AIIB and $US150million from the World Bank, and is intended to support Government’s reform programme by strengthening economic resilience, improving public financial management and creating a more enabling environment for private-sector growth.

Minister for Finance Immanuel Esrom said the financing was not entirely made up of loans, with the package including both loan and grant funding.

He said the AIIB component had already been allocated in the budget and would support government programs over the current and previous financial years.

“The loans come with a purpose,” he said.

“This support complements our commitment to prudent fiscal management, climate resilience and creating a more enabling environment for businesses and investment.”

Mr Esrom said the loan portion was policy-based financing, continuing support first introduced after the COVID-19 pandemic to strengthen Fiji’s financial systems and climate resilience.

Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said discussions with the AIIB and World Bank formed part of the Government’s broader infrastructure development plans, with project proposals still being finalised by the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Works.

Addressing criticism that the Government was increasing national debt through borrowing, Mr Rabuka said no loan agreements had been signed yet and discussions were still taking place with potential development partners.

“Any future borrowing would be considered alongside the Government’s debt repayment commitments to ensure they remained sustainable,” Mr Rabuka said.

Meanwhile, AIIB president Zou Jiayi reaffirmed the bank’s long-term commitment to Fiji.

item.title: Tough new laws – Fines rise to $50k under proposed FCCC Bill
item.description: THE proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 increases fines 50-fold and expands search and seizure powers for the FCCC. Individuals who obstruct Competition and Consumer Commission investigations or refuse to comply with lawful notices could face fines of up to $50,000 and 10 years’ imprisonment under the proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026, a dramatic increase fr
item.content:encoded:
THE proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 increases fines 50-fold and expands search and seizure powers for the FCCC.

Individuals who obstruct Competition and Consumer Commission investigations or refuse to comply with lawful notices could face fines of up to $50,000 and 10 years’ imprisonment under the proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026, a dramatic increase from previous penalties of $1000, later increased to $5000, under existing legislation.

The draft Bill, now open for nationwide public consultation, introduces sweeping new enforcement powers, significantly tougher penalties and expanded authority for Commission officers to investigate anti-competitive conduct and consumer protection offences.

Among the most significant changes is the increase in penalties for non-compliance with investigation notices and obstruction of Commission officers. Under the proposal, individuals who fail to comply with investigation notices without a reasonable excuse, provide false or misleading information, destroy evidence or obstruct investigations could be fined up to $50,000, imprisoned for up to 10 years, or both. Companies could face fines of up to $500,000.

The proposed penalties represent a substantial escalation from previous laws, where maximum fines stood at $1000 before later increasing to $5000.

The Bill would also considerably strengthen the Commission’s investigative powers.

Commission officers would be authorised to enter and search premises with the occupier’s consent, under a court-issued warrant, or without a warrant in urgent situations where there are reasonable grounds to believe evidence could be lost, destroyed or tampered with.

They would also be empowered to search individuals in public places without a warrant where it is urgently necessary to prevent the destruction or loss of evidence.

To address the growing importance of electronic evidence, the Bill would allow commission officers to examine computers, copy electronic records and access documents stored remotely through computer systems.

Where officers believe digital evidence is at risk, they would also be able to secure computers and other electronic equipment for up to 72 hours while expert assistance is obtained or forensic examinations are carried out.

The proposed legislation allows officers to lock away equipment, place it under guard or take any other reasonable steps necessary to preserve evidence.

If additional time is required, officers would have to apply to a magistrate for an extension, with any continued detention of equipment requiring judicial approval.

The Bill also modernises the process for obtaining search warrants.

Judges, magistrates and justices of the peace would be able to issue warrants authorising searches of homes, businesses, vehicles, vessels and aircraft. Warrants would remain valid for a maximum of seven days and could be applied for electronically, by telephone or other appropriate means where appearing in person is impractical.

The draft legislation also introduces safeguards for people under investigation.

Before questioning anyone who may face prosecution or financial penalties, Commission officers would be required to advise them of their right to remain silent, that they are not required to answer questions, and that anything they say may be used as evidence in future proceedings.

Any evidence obtained without providing those warnings would generally be inadmissible in criminal or financial penalty proceedings.

The Commission would continue to be required to investigate public complaints but could decline to proceed where complaints are considered frivolous, vexatious, lacking substance or not a reasonable use of resources. The Minister would also retain the power to refer matters directly to the Commission for investigation.

Public consultations on the proposed Competition and Consumer Commission Bill 2026 began last night in Suva.

item.title: FCCC angers growers
item.description: GROWERS operating mechanical harvesters could be forced to ground their machines under the new $20.52 rate announced by the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission. Reduced by $4.11 from $24.63, growers heavily dependent on the harvesters have called on authorities to look into what they say could put place more pressure on the industry.
item.content:encoded:
GROWERS operating mechanical harvesters could be forced to ground their machines under the new $20.52 rate announced by the Fijian Competition and Consumer Commission.

Reduced by $4.11 from $24.63, growers heavily dependent on the harvesters have called on authorities to look into what they say could put place more pressure on the industry.

Lautoka Sugarcane Producers Association chairperson Bala Dass said there was no consultation carried out between industry stakeholders and FCCC.

“This is the kind of problems that is putting the sugar industry further down,” said Mr Dass.

“They did not conduct any consultations with the farmers with the Sugar Cane Growers Council, the Sugar Industry Tribunal. With immediate effect they put it to $20.52 and we the machine operators and the farmers are not happy with it. We are going to have a meeting soon to discuss this because this could force us to ground our machines.

“We will not make any profit from this new rate. We will fork out money from our own pockets because the maintenance costs are too high.”

Sugar Cane Growers Council CEO Vimal Dutt said while growers hiring the machines stood benefit from the new rate, cooperatives made up of farmers were on the losing end of the new fee.

“On one side, the grower will benefit because they are paying a cheaper rate but on the other side, we have our cooperative that has concerns about the rate being too low,” said Mr Dutt.

“It is a concern and we need to have a discussion about it with all of the relevant stakeholders.”

In a statement, FCCC explained following an independent assessment and the recent decline in fuel prices noted in Fiji, the Commission revised the Mechanical Harvesting Rates by 16.7 per cent, decreasing from the current authorised interim rates of $24.63 per tonne to $20.52 per tonne.

“These interim measures are intended to ensure that the authorised rates remain aligned with current operating costs while supporting the continued sustainability of harvesting and transportation services.”
